concept: Engram and n-gram embedding tables read from disk per token
summary: Engram (arXiv 2601.07372) retrieves static embeddings for suffix n-grams by deterministic hashing, using tokenizer compression and K hash heads per n-gram order, then fuses them with the hidden state through context-aware gating.

facts.text: Engram (arXiv 2601.07372) retrieves static embeddings for suffix n-grams by deterministic hashing, using tokenizer compression and K hash heads per n-gram order, then fuses them with the hidden state through context-aware gating.
The published 27B configs use n-gram orders 2 and 3, 8 heads, d_mem 1280 and Engram layers 2 and 15.
The hash is described as a lightweight multiplicative-XOR function into prime-sized per-head tables.
Row indices are fixed once the token sequence is known and can be computed before the corresponding layer executes, so reads can be prefetched and overlapped with earlier blocks.

The paper measured a 100B-parameter Engram table in host DRAM on one NVIDIA H800 with nano-vLLM: 4B dense baseline 9,031.62 tok/s versus 8,858.28 tok/s with offload, 8B dense 6,315.52 versus 6,140.02, a worst-case penalty of 2.8%.
The paper's benchmark forced all retrievals over PCIe from host memory and used no locality cache, and the authors call it a conservative baseline.
The paper describes a multi-level cache hierarchy (HBM or DRAM for hot rows, NVMe SSD for the long tail) as a design option motivated by Zipfian n-gram frequency, and reports no NVMe measurement.
The paper states the effective communication volume per step scales with the number of activated slots rather than the total table size.
The paper's ablation says modeling quality favors an early Engram layer while system latency hiding favors a later one, so placement must satisfy both.
The official deepseek-ai/Engram repository contains the paper, figures and one standalone demo script (engram_demo_v1.py) and no inference or offload runtime.
In XNU, F_NOCACHE sets VNOCACHE_DATA, which makes the cluster read path set IO_NOCACHE, which disables read-ahead and stops the read from taking a page reference.

With IO_NOCACHE a user-space read becomes a candidate for the direct I/O path (cluster_io_type picks IO_DIRECT when the iovec is long enough), and in the buffered copy path the pages are aborted with UPL_ABORT_DUMP_PAGES instead of being committed to the cache.
ds4's separate F_NOCACHE plus F_RDAHEAD 0 descriptor for Engram rows therefore matches what the kernel does: no read-ahead and no cache residency for single-row reads.
Engram row reads on a Mac cannot hit the page cache after the first read when F_NOCACHE is set, so every row read is an SSD read, unlike the warm-cache expert reads in Flash-MoE.
F_NOCACHE does not apply to file pages faulted through mmap, so a runtime that maps the Engram table gets page-cache residency and reclaim behavior instead.
On a Mac the paper's prefetch window (one transformer block of compute) must cover an NVMe random-read latency instead of a PCIe-from-DRAM copy, so the 2.8% overhead figure does not transfer.
No source found measures Engram or n-gram table reads on an Apple SSD in rows per second, bytes per token or latency per row.
